payload.name: Extract all enumerated activities
payload.description: When extracting construction memories from a message where the speaker lists multiple distinct activities, experiences, or facts in one utterance, use this skill to ensure each listed item is captured.
content: During extraction, when a single user message enumerates multiple distinct activities or facts (e.g., studying, attending workshops, networking, presenting), create a memory candidate for each distinct item rather than only the most prominent or recent one.

Before adding an event memory that describes what someone did, scan the full source message for explicit lists and include every listed activity; if the activities are independent, prefer separate candidates so no listed fact is lost.

candidates.solves: Candidate extraction captured only the most salient activity from a message that explicitly enumerated several activities (studying, workshops, networking, presenting), so omitted facts were never stored. This pattern recurs when a single speaker message lists multiple distinct activities; extracting each enumerated item separately prevents incomplete memories. Applies to extraction of explicit lists, not to inferring unstated activities or merging existing memories.

payload.name: Preserve explicit outcomes in memory extraction
payload.description: Use when constructing memories from messages that state a specific achievement or result, ensuring the concrete outcome is retained rather than replaced by a generic summary.
content: During extraction, if the source explicitly states that someone achieved a specific outcome (e.g., 'reached their goals', 'won a competition'), include that concrete achievement in the memory content. Do not let a broader paraphrase (e.g., 'saw their growth') replace the explicitly mentioned result.

candidates.solves: When drafting a memory from an utterance, the model often over-summarizes explicitly stated concrete outcomes into vague terms, losing the fact needed for later questions. This rule applies to any extraction where the speaker mentions a specific achievement or result; it is not for unsupported inferences or implied outcomes.

payload.name: Preserve ordinal and temporal cues for creative works
payload.description: When extracting memories about a user's creative work (e.g., screenplay, book, art) and the conversation includes an ordinal like 'third' or a date/time reference, include both the ordinal and the inferred event date in the memory.
content: During extraction from messages about creative projects, if the speaker references an ordinal (first, second, third, etc.) or a start/completion time, record that ordinal as part of the artifact's identity and set the event's world_start to the message date when it indicates the start.
When adding or updating a creative-work memory, include the ordinal (e.g., 'third screenplay') in the content; do not summarize it away into a generic activity statement.

If the user confirms an ordinal in a reply (e.g., 'Yep! ...'), treat the confirmation as explicit evidence and encode it in the same event or profile memory, along with the date context from the session.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline sometimes summarizes creative-work discussions into generic profile/event memories, dropping ordinal identifiers (e.g., 'third', 'second') and concrete temporal references that are explicitly stated or contextually grounded in the conversation. This rule applies whenever a user mentions completing or working on a creative artifact with an ordinal or time cue; the memory should capture the ordinal and, if the surrounding session provides a date, that date as the work's start or completion time. It is not meant for cases where the ordinal or time is absent or ambiguous.

payload.name: Preserve source or discovery details in extraction
payload.description: When extracting memories from a user message, if the message states how a person heard about or discovered an event, keep that detail in a memory.
content: When building memory candidates from a message, treat how the person learned about or discovered an event (e.g., saw a flyer, heard from a friend, read an ad) as a durable fact. Include it in the event memory or create a separate memory for it, even when the main action is something else. Do not drop this detail during extraction or later updates.

candidates.solves: During extraction, when a message states how the person learned about or discovered an event (e.g., saw a flyer, heard from a friend, read an ad), that detail is often omitted when the main action is captured, so later questions like "how did X hear about Y?" cannot be answered. Preserving source/discovery details as part of the event memory or as a separate memory generalizes across workshops, classes, sales, and announcements; it does not require storing transient or non-durable context.

payload.name: Extract_Multiple_Facts_Per_Message
payload.description: Use during construction extraction when a user message contains multiple distinct events, facts, or state changes; create a separate candidate for each rather than only the most salient one.
content: During candidate extraction, treat each explicit durable fact or event in a message as a separate candidate; do not let one salient topic (e.g., a trip) suppress another explicitly stated fact (e.g., a vehicle breakdown).
If a message contrasts two items or time periods (old vs new, before vs after), capture each side's state separately so that later questions can retrieve either fact.
Before finalizing a memory for a message, scan the raw text for every independent claim about the subject's possessions, plans, or experiences and ensure each is represented in some candidate.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause was that extraction produced one candidate from a message containing two distinct user facts: a trip and a separate breakdown of a different item, so the breakdown was never stored. The abstract failure is single-candidate dominance, where a more prominent event causes other explicit durable facts in the same message to be omitted. This rule applies to any construction session where a message bundles multiple independent facts, events, or state changes, and prevents loss of evidence needed for later questions.

payload.name: Extract explicit relationship duration statements
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a speaker states an explicit duration for a relationship or group membership, generate a relationship memory candidate even if the statement is conversational.
content: During candidate extraction, identify explicit duration phrases attached to relationship or group-membership predicates, such as 'were teammates for X years', 'worked together since Y', or 'have known each other for Z years'.

For each identified phrase, create a relationship-type candidate memory that records the relationship and its stated duration; do not skip it because the sentence also contains conversational filler or a return question.
If the duration is given relative to a time mentioned in the message/session, resolve it to the session timestamp before finalizing the candidate.

candidates.solves: The construction run skipped extraction of a clear relationship-duration statement, leaving no memory to answer later questions. The reusable mechanism is that explicit durations attached to relationships are easy to overlook in conversational replies. This rule applies whenever a speaker states how long a relationship or group membership lasted; it does not apply when duration is only implied or must be inferred from context.

payload.name: Preserve explicit life-stage and duration facts
payload.description: When a message describes a person's history across explicit stages (schools, teams, careers) or states a duration, use specific stage/duration facts in memory extraction instead of a vague summary.
content: During extraction, identify explicit life-stage or level mentions (e.g., middle school, high school, college, professional) and duration phrases (e.g., for four years) in the source message.
Extract each such stage and duration as separate, memory-worthy facts; do not merge them into a generic phrase like 'since childhood.'
If a later message adds a stage or duration for the same topic, add or update the corresponding fact rather than relying on prior summary.

candidates.solves: A memory extraction often fails when a person's narrative is summarized as a general trajectory (e.g., played since childhood) and explicit educational or team stages and durations are dropped. This skill enforces extracting each explicit stage (middle school, high school, college, professional) and stated duration as separate durable facts. It applies to any future construction pass over biographical timeline statements in conversations, but does not infer stages or durations that are not explicitly stated.

payload.name: Extract Explicit Advice as Preference Memory
payload.description: Use during candidate extraction when a participant explicitly gives advice, recommendations, or criteria in response to another participant's question.
content: When extracting candidates from a session, treat explicit advice, recommendations, or criteria given by one participant to another as preference candidates, even if the advice is not about the speaker's own current plans or events.
Store the core advice compactly as a preference memory attributed to the advice-giver, and link it to the source message.
This rule applies only to candidate extraction; it does not require a separate CRUD operation and does not apply to casual or non-advice remarks.

candidates.solves: Explicit advice messages are ingested without producing a memory candidate, so guidance is lost. The mechanism is overlooking recommendation statements during extraction when they are not about the speaker's own plans/events. This applies when one participant gives advice or criteria to another; do not apply to non-advice casual remarks. Extract the core guidance as a preference memory attributed to the speaker and linked to the source message.

payload.name: Extract first-person explanatory preferences and states
payload.description: When a speaker directly answers a question about why they made a choice or how they feel about something, extract the stated reason/preference/state as a memory candidate even if it lacks explicit preference wording.
content: During extraction, treat direct first-person answers to 'why' or feeling questions as evidence of durable preference or state.
Create a `preference` candidate for stated likes, choices, or motivations; create a `state` candidate for current feelings or conditions.
Do not require phrases like 'I like' or 'I prefer'; explanatory wording is sufficient.
Ensure the candidate is source-linked to the message.

candidates.solves: Diagnosed cause: no candidate memory was created when a speaker directly explained her reason for a decision, leaving durable preference facts absent. The failure mechanism is extraction omitting first-person explanatory statements that convey preferences or states when not phrased as 'I like'. This applies to future answers that explain motivations, feelings, or choices; it does not apply to third-party descriptions, hypotheticals, or already-covered facts.

payload.name: Extract colloquial preference and activity statements as memory candidates
payload.description: During candidate extraction, when a speaker uses informal positive/negative language (e.g., 'go crazy for', 'love', 'hate') to state a preference or activity, create a candidate even if the phrasing is not formal.
content: During candidate extraction, treat colloquial statements of preference or activity as explicit candidates. Phrases like 'go crazy for', 'love', 'hate', 'can't stand', 'prefer', or 'enjoy' signal durable likes, dislikes, or recurring activities.

Extract the subject, the liked/disliked item or activity, and any relevant context (such as location or time) into a compact preference/event candidate, even if the sentence is casual or conversational.
Do not skip extraction solely because the statement is informal or appears in a chatty reply; explicit sentiment about an entity is still a memory-worthy fact.

candidates.solves: Users often state stable preferences or activities informally ('go crazy for', 'love', 'hate'); extraction may skip these because wording is casual, so the fact never enters memory. Apply whenever a speaker explicitly expresses positive/negative preference or recurring activity, regardless of tone, during candidate extraction. This transfers across pets, people, foods, hobbies, and similar preference topics.

payload.name: Extract explicit preference statements
payload.description: When a participant explicitly states what they find beautiful, like, love, or prefer, create a `preference` candidate during extraction even if the statement appears inside a suggestion or plan.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly evaluates an entity positively (e.g., 'X is beautiful', 'I love Y'), create a `preference` candidate with the speaker as subject and the entity as object.
Do not skip the evaluation because it is embedded in a suggestion or plan (e.g., 'How about going there? The colors are so beautiful!'); the evaluative clause is still a durable preference.

candidates.solves: The failed fact was an explicit preference statement embedded in a suggestion, skipped at ingestion because it read as planning language. The reusable mechanism: evaluative clauses inside casual suggestion or plan wording still express the speaker's preference and must be extracted. Applies when a participant states what they find beautiful, like, love, or prefer; not to hypothetical conditionals or generic statements without an asserted preference.

payload.name: ExtractPreferencesFromAffectiveEndorsements
payload.description: When a speaker answers a direct question about a favorite or preference using positive evaluative language (e.g., 'really speaks to me', 'so expressive', 'love it') instead of explicit 'my favorite is', extract the endorsed item as a preference memory.
content: During candidate extraction, treat a first-person response to a favorite/preference question as a preference candidate even if it lacks the phrase 'favorite'; phrases like 'really speaks to me', 'I love', or 'so expressive' are sufficient evidence when they directly follow such a question.
Create a preference/profile memory for the endorsed entity with the speaker as the subject; do not wait for an explicit 'my favorite is X' formulation.
Do not apply to statements about others' preferences, hypothetical likes/dislikes, or mere mentions of an activity without affective endorsement.

candidates.solves: The construction pipeline missed a durable preference memory because it required explicit 'favorite' wording and ignored affective endorsements given as direct answers to preference questions. This skill teaches extraction to recognize first-person evaluative responses as preference evidence, preventing missing profile memories across any domain whenever such responses occur.

payload.name: Include all explicit reasons in preference extraction
payload.description: When extracting a profile or preference memory, if the source explicitly gives multiple reasons for liking, disliking, or choosing something, include all distinct reasons in the memory content.
content: During extraction, if a speaker explicitly lists multiple reasons or traits for a preference or choice, capture every distinct reason in the candidate memory content; do not drop any reason because another reason seems more salient.
Before adding or updating a profile/preference memory, check the source message for every stated reason and ensure the memory content reflects all of them.

candidates.solves: The extraction stage sometimes records only a subset of explicitly stated reasons for a preference, so later questions about omitted reasons cannot be answered from memory. This rule applies whenever a source message lists multiple distinct reasons or traits for a like/dislike or choice: the extracted profile memory must include every explicit reason.

payload.name: Extract explicit stated preferences from conversational replies
payload.description: When a user explicitly names an item they like or calls it a favorite, during extraction create a preference/event candidate even if the statement is an enthusiastic answer to a question or uses informal wording.
content: During extraction, treat direct, unambiguous statements of liking or preference (e.g., 'X is my favorite', 'I love X', 'Definitely X!') as candidates for a preference memory, or an event memory when tied to a specific occasion, regardless of whether they occur in response to a question or in a casual/emphatic tone.

If the user names a specific item as their favorite, record it as its own candidate rather than embedding it only inside a broader summary, so future queries about that item can be answered from memory.
Do not skip a candidate solely because the mention is brief, colloquial, or part of a conversation about other topics.

candidates.solves: Construction extraction sometimes omits an explicit user statement of liking because it is phrased as a casual or emphatic reply to a question, causing later queries about that item to remain unanswered. This Skill ensures direct, unambiguous preference statements are always extracted as preference or event candidates, independent of the topic, so future questions about any named liked item are answerable.

payload.name: Extract explicit first-person preference statements as preference memories
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states a personal preference, favorite item, or like/dislike, use this during extraction to create a preference memory candidate even if the message contains other topics.
content: During extraction, when a speaker explicitly states a personal preference, favorite, or like/dislike (e.g., 'my favorite dish is X', 'I love Y'), create a preference memory candidate even if the statement is embedded in a longer message about other topics or follows a question from another participant.
Record the speaker as the subject of the preference and use the 'preference' memory type; do not require the statement to be repeated or confirmed before extraction.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that an explicit 'my favorite dish is lasagna' statement produced no extraction candidates, so the preference was never stored. This indicates the extraction stage can overlook self-disclosed preferences when they appear in longer conversational turns. The rule generalizes to any explicit first-person preference/favorite/like-dislike statement and applies to future construction runs where such statements appear; it stops at implicit preferences or third-party statements that require inference.

payload.name: Separate General Preference from Specific Event
payload.description: When a message contains both a concrete occurrence (e.g., visited a cafe) and a general statement about a recurring preference or habit (e.g., love to discover new places to eat), create separate candidates rather than merging them.
content: During extraction, if a message contains both a concrete event/occurrence and an explicit general statement about a recurring preference or habit (signaled by phrases like 'love to', 'usually', 'always'), create a separate preference candidate for the general statement and an event/state candidate for the concrete occurrence. Do not let the specific event absorb the general statement.

candidates.solves: The extractor collapsed a speaker's general statement ('love to discover new places to eat') into the specific event (visited a cafe), losing the durable preference. The abstract mechanism is conflating a stated recurring preference with its concrete instance during extraction. This rule applies whenever a message contains both a specific occurrence and an explicit general habit/preference statement; it does not apply to purely one-time, non-recurring statements.

payload.name: Extract explicit subjective feelings as memories
payload.description: When a speaker explicitly states a subjective feeling or evaluation about an activity or thing (e.g., 'it's magical'), create a preference or state memory during candidate extraction.
content: During candidate extraction, explicitly monitor for utterances where a speaker states a personal feeling or evaluation about an activity, event, or object, often signaled by evaluative adjectives (magical, amazing, exciting, etc.) or phrases (I love, I enjoy, it makes me feel).

When found, create a preference memory (or state memory if clearly temporary) for that speaker, capturing the object and the stated feeling. Do not skip these statements even when embedded in longer supportive or motivational messages.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed failure was that an explicit self-report of a feeling (Gina describing dance as 'magical') generated no memory candidate. The abstract mechanism is that subjective evaluative utterances are often skipped during extraction. This skill applies to any future session where a speaker explicitly characterizes an experience or object with an evaluative adjective or phrase, ensuring such statements are stored as durable preference/state memories. It does not apply to purely factual statements or unsupported opinions.

payload.name: Extract explicit key principles as preferences
payload.description: When a conversation message explicitly states a person's key principle, value, or strategy about their work or customers, extract it as a preference memory during construction.
content: During candidate extraction, treat explicit belief or value statements as preference candidates, even if phrased as encouragement or general advice.
Record the speaker, the belief/value expressed, and the source message; do not require an associated event or plan before extracting.
Do not extend this rule to implied or inferred opinions; the statement must explicitly articulate the principle.

candidates.solves: The diagnosed cause is that an explicit statement of a speaker's key principle (e.g., that creating a special experience is what makes customers feel welcome) generated no extraction candidate and was never stored. The reusable mechanism is to capture such explicit belief/principle statements as preference memories during extraction. This applies to future conversations where participants state a value or strategy; it does not apply to inferred attitudes or unstated implications.

operations.name: Extract All Enumerated Facts from Multi-Fact Messages
operations.description: Use when a single message explicitly lists multiple distinct activities, facts, or events that must each be captured.
content: During candidate extraction, scan the full source message for explicit enumerations (lists, multiple clauses, or distinct claims). Create a separate candidate for each distinct item or fact; do not let one salient topic suppress another.
If a message contrasts two items or time periods, capture each side's state separately so later questions can retrieve either fact.
Before finalizing a candidate list, verify every explicitly enumerated element is represented in some candidate; do not add inferred items.
